extracted.intended_audience: paleobotanists, paleontologists, naturalists, and scientifically literate readers interested in Paleozoic plant evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria used to identify, classify, and infer affinities of Devonian–Carboniferous fossil plants from morphological and anatomical evidence. Emphasises what kinds of preservation and characters (wood, cones, sporangia, fronds, seeds) are considered decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for seed-plants (Upper Devonian)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best proof of the presence of seed-plants in the Upper Devonian is to be found in the occurrence of petrified stems, which, from their organisation, must presumably have belonged to advanced Gymnosperms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petrified stems with gymnosperm-like organisation (e.g., Callixylon) are taken as primary evidence; wood anatomy such as pits localised in definite groups and highly differentiated secondary wood support identification as advanced seed-plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wood anatomy (Callixylon example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genus Callixylon ... has a peculiar and beautiful structure in the secondary wood, the pits being localised in definite groups. The wood appears more highly differentiated than that of most living Conifers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive features of secondary wood (pit localisation, degree of differentiation) are diagnostic characters for affiliating fossil stems with particular gymnosperm groups; detailed anatomical comparison to extant analogues is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing true ferns from fern-like seed-plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Where anatomical characters are available, we find no approximation whatever between the two groups. Pteridosperms and Ferns at all times show themselves perfectly distinct, whenever our knowledge admits of an adequate comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on habit or frond appearance; anatomical evidence (vascular structure, reproductive organs) is required to separate true ferns from seed-ferns (pteridosperms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of true ferns via Zygopterid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Dawson’s Asteropteris ... has the structure of a Zygopterid, a group well known from Carboniferous rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frond and internal structural characters that match known Zygopterid anatomy (vascular patterns, petiole structure) are used to identify true fern affinities in Devonian specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of heterospory and seed-like fructification in Lycopods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lower Carboniferous Lycopods ... cones constantly (so far as observed) heterosporous, with an extreme differentiation of the two kinds of spore, but some of them even developed a kind of seed ... a single megaspore only came to maturity, constituting the embryo-sac, while an integument, like a seed-coat, grew up round the sporangium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterospory, extreme differentiation between micro- and megaspores, presence of an integument around the sporangium, and seed-like structures (Lepidocarpon) are key characters for recognising seed-bearing or near-seed reproductive strategies in fossil Lycopods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prothallus/prospective archegonium as reproductive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The prothallus is sometimes well preserved, both in the seed-like bodies and in the more ordinary megaspores. ... Dr. Gordon has recorded a perfectly typical archegonium, showing that the details of reproduction in these old Lycopods were the same as in their modern heterosporous representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preservation of prothalli and archegonia provides direct evidence of reproductive biology and homology with modern groups; such finds strongly inform taxonomic placement and life-cycle inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring affinities from leaf and cone morphology (Sphenophylls, Horsetails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sphenophyllums ... whorled leaves ... deeply cut. ... As regards the affinities of the Sphenophylls, some relation to the Horsetail stock seems evident, as indicated by the whorled leaves, the general organisation of the cones, and the detailed structure of the sporangia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of gross morphology (leaf arrangement, degree of leaf division) and reproductive organ structure (cone organisation, sporangial detail) to infer relationships between fossil groups (e.g., sphenophylls and equisetaleans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of cone and sporangium characters (annulus, synangium, sterile appendages)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Stauropteris sporangia were borne singly ... had no annulus ... In Diplolabis the sporangia are grouped in a sort of synangium, while those associated with Botryopteris have a biseriate annulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence or absence of an annulus, grouping into synangia, and arrangement of sterile appendages are diagnostic for distinguishing families and tracing affinities among fossil ferns and fern-like plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting frond morphology (quadriseriate pinnae, plane orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The morphology of the frond. Even where there were only two series of pinne ... their plane was not parallel to that of the main rachis, but at right angles to it. Moreover ... the pinne were in four rows, two rows on each side, a condition unexampled in ordinary leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual frond architectures (e.g., quadriseriate rows, right-angle pinnae orientation) are significant taxonomic characters; detailed morphological description of fronds helps place fossils within or apart from extant lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of seeds by association and anatomical similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautifully organised seed (Spherostoma, Benson), obviously related to that of the Upper Carboniferous Lyginopteris, is found in close association with Heterangium Grievii and probably belonged to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeds are found in close association with vegetative or wood remains and share anatomical features, they may be attributed to that plant; such associative evidence supports linking dispersed organs to parent taxa but should be used cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vascular cylinder and petiole anatomy in family-level diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: The vascular cylinder of the stem shows some differentiation of the wood into a central region ... and a wide outer zone of larger elements. The petiole always has a peculiar structure, with a bilateral strand (often of complex form) giving off branch-bundles to the right and left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal stem vascular patterns (central core vs outer zone) and distinctive petiole vascular organisation are employed to diagnose families (e.g., Zygopterids) and to reassess supposed primitive/simple taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in phylogenetic inference (monophyletic vs polyphyletic hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some botanists believe that the higher plants may have had a common source ... while others hold that the main phyla have always been distinct ... The existence of these rival monophyletic and polyphyletic hypotheses ... shows how little definite knowledge of the evolutionary history we possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise limits of evidence: avoid strong phylogenetic conclusions in absence of transitional data; consider competing hypotheses and treat affinity claims as provisional pending more material.
